title: The Kahun papyrus on women's health
summary: A papyrus from the town of Lahun in Egypt, written around 1800 BCE, sets out diagnoses and treatments for gynaecological complaints, fertility and pregnancy. It is the oldest surviving Egyptian medical papyrus.
explanation:
The papyrus was excavated at el-Lahun, near the Faiyum, by Flinders Petrie in 1889 and is now in the Petrie Museum at University College London (UC 32057). It dates from the Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom.

The text is divided into short sections, each describing a woman's complaint, how to recognise it and how to treat it, with remedies applied to the body or taken by mouth rather than surgery. It also covers fertility, pregnancy and contraception.

Older medical texts exist elsewhere: a Sumerian medical text from around 2000 BCE is known from Mesopotamia.

date.basis: Dated on palaeographic and archaeological grounds to the Twelfth Dynasty (Middle Kingdom), which ended c. 1773 BCE.

whatChanged: Preserves the earliest systematic written guidance on women's reproductive health from Egypt.
whyItMattered: Shows that maternal and reproductive health was a distinct field of medical knowledge nearly four thousand years ago.
limitations: Its explanations reflect Egyptian ideas of the body, such as the womb causing symptoms elsewhere; many remedies would not be effective.
Being the oldest surviving Egyptian medical papyrus says nothing about where such knowledge began.

sources.citation: Science in Ancient Egypt (Saxon Academy of Sciences, Leipzig). Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus (UC 32057), with bibliography including Collier M, Quirke S. The UCL Lahun Papyri (BAR International Series 1209, 2004), 58–64.
sources.supports: Inventory UC 32057 at the Petrie Museum; findspot el-Lahun; Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty; text type handbook.

sources.citation: Garrison–Morton (HistoryofMedicine.com), entry 7011: The Petrie papyri. Hieratic papyri from Kahun and Gurob, ed. F. Ll. Griffith (1898).
sources.supports: c. 1800 BCE; found at El-Lahun by Petrie in 1889; translated by Griffith (1893); concerns gynaecological diseases, fertility, pregnancy and contraception.

sources.citation: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative. Medical texts (CDLI Wiki).
sources.supports: The oldest known complete medical text, from about 2000 BC, is in Sumerian.

title: The Edwin Smith papyrus: injuries examined case by case
summary: An Egyptian papyrus copied around 1600 BCE presents 48 cases of wounds and fractures, each with examination, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment. It includes the earliest known written descriptions of the brain's surface and of spinal injury.
explanation:
The scroll is named after the American dealer Edwin Smith, who bought it near Luxor in 1862; it is now held by the New York Academy of Medicine. It was copied around 1600 BCE from an older text whose date is uncertain.

Its 48 cases are ordered from the skull down to the chest and upper arm, and each follows a fixed formula: a description of the injury, the diagnosis, a prognosis and the treatment, with explanatory notes. Several cases describe skull fractures exposing the brain and its coverings, and injuries of the neck that cause paralysis.

The main text is strikingly free of magic, though spells and recipes appear on the other side of the papyrus.

date.basis: The surviving copy is dated to about 1600 BCE. The original it was copied from is older; estimates range widely and are uncertain.

locations.name: Thebes region, where the papyrus was bought in 1862
locations.role: Acquired near Luxor; original findspot and place of writing unknown

locationNote: The papyrus was bought, not excavated, so the marker shows where it surfaced rather than where it was written.

people.name: An unknown Egyptian author and later copyist

whatChanged: Shows a structured, observation-based approach to injuries, including the judgement that some cases should not be treated.
whyItMattered: It is the oldest known surgical treatise and a key witness to Egyptian clinical reasoning.
limitations: It is a copy; the date and authorship of the original are unknown, and the 1862 purchase means its findspot is unrecorded.
Claims that it reflects a 'scientific' medicine separate from magic are partly modern framing; the same scroll contains spells.

sources.citation: New York Academy of Medicine. Edwin Smith Surgical Papyrus.
sources.supports: Created about 1600 BCE in hieratic; 48 cases of wounds and trauma in a fixed formula; magical spells on the reverse; held by NYAM.

sources.citation: Stiefel M, et al. The Edwin Smith Papyrus: the birth of analytical thinking in medicine and otolaryngology. Laryngoscope 2006 (PubMed record).
sources.supports: Discovered in 1862 outside Luxor; a copy of an earlier text; 48 cases, mostly traumatic injuries.

sources.citation: Minagar A, et al. The Edwin Smith surgical papyrus: description and analysis of the earliest case of aphasia. Journal of Medical Biography 2003;11(2):114–117.
sources.supports: First written use of the word for brain; earliest descriptions of the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.

sources.citation: The Edwin Smith papyrus: a clinical reappraisal of the oldest known document on spinal injuries (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: Seventeenth century BCE; six of the 48 cases concern the spine.

sources.citation: Management of fractures of the humerus in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome: an historical review (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: Copied circa 1600 BC; 48 cases topographically ordered from the skull to the chest and upper arm.

sources.citation: Spinal cord injury: past, present, and future (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: Purchased by Edwin Smith in Luxor in 1862; translated by Breasted, published 1930; six cervical spine cases, two with spinal cord injury.

title: Babylon's Diagnostic Handbook is edited
summary: Around the mid-eleventh century BCE the Babylonian scholar Esagil-kīn-apli produced a standard edition of Sakikkû, a long series of tablets linking symptoms to diagnoses and prognoses.
explanation:
Mesopotamian healers had been writing down medical knowledge for centuries. Esagil-kīn-apli, chief scholar to King Adad-apla-iddina, gathered and edited the diagnostic omen series known as Sakikkû, 'symptoms', creating the version that later scribes copied. His own catalogue explaining the new edition survives in Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian copies.

Each entry follows a conditional formula: if a patient shows certain signs, then the diagnosis or outcome is this. The handbook covers symptoms throughout the body and records disease names, prognosis and supposed causes, which often included divine or demonic agency alongside natural explanations.

The work shows diagnosis organised as a systematic body of knowledge long before Greek medicine.

date.basis: During the reign of Adad-apla-iddina, as named in Esagil-kīn-apli's catalogue; reign dates themselves vary slightly between chronologies.

locations.name: Babylonia
locations.role: Region where the edition was made; copies survive from Assyria and Babylonia

people.name: Esagil-kīn-apli
people.role: Chief scholar (ummânu) who edited the series

whatChanged: Created a standardised reference that tied observable signs to diagnosis and prognosis.
whyItMattered: One of the earliest large-scale systematisations of diagnosis, and a reminder that diagnostic reasoning did not begin in Greece.
limitations: The handbook mixes clinical observation with divination; its causes are often supernatural.
Esagil-kīn-apli edited an existing tradition rather than composing it from scratch.

sources.citation: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative. Medical texts (CDLI Wiki).
sources.supports: Diagnostic Handbook by Esagil-kīn-apli during the reign of Adad-apla-iddina (1067–1046 BC); symptoms, disease names, prognosis and causation; casuistic formula; earlier Middle Babylonian diagnostic texts.

sources.citation: Schmidtchen E. Esagil-kīn-apli's catalogue of Sakikkû and Alamdimmû. Chapter in an edited volume (De Gruyter).
sources.supports: Catalogue names King Adad-apla-iddina; editorial work in the middle of the 11th century BCE; Heeßel's edition of the Diagnostic Handbook.

title: 'On the Sacred Disease' argues epilepsy is natural
summary: A treatise in the Hippocratic collection, written around 450–400 BCE by an unknown author, insists that epilepsy is no more divine than any other disease and that its seat is the brain.
explanation:
Epilepsy was widely called the 'sacred disease' and treated with purifications and charms. The author of this short treatise attacked that view, arguing that people called the disease divine only because they did not understand it.

He described seizures from observation, loss of voice, foaming at the mouth, clenched hands and loss of awareness, and located their cause in the brain, which he regarded as the organ of thought and feeling. His mechanism, phlegm blocking passages from the brain, came from humoral theory and has not survived, but the insistence on natural causes did.

The treatise belongs to the Hippocratic Corpus, a collection of writings by many authors traditionally linked to Hippocrates of Kos. Its author is not known, and earlier thinkers such as Alcmaeon of Croton had already identified the brain as the seat of intelligence.

date.basis: Usually dated to the second half of the fifth century BCE on stylistic and historical grounds.

locations.name: Greek-speaking Aegean world
locations.role: Author and place of writing unknown; the Corpus is traditionally linked to Kos

whatChanged: Argued explicitly that a feared condition had natural, brain-based causes rather than divine ones.
whyItMattered: An early challenge to supernatural explanations of disease and to the stigma attached to epilepsy, which nonetheless persisted for centuries.
limitations: The proposed mechanism (phlegm from the brain) was wrong.
Attribution to Hippocrates himself is traditional, not established.
Natural and supernatural explanations coexisted in many traditions, including Mesopotamian and Egyptian medicine.

sources.citation: Theodore WH, in: Third International Congress on Epilepsy, Brain and Mind, part 1. Epilepsy & Behavior (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: First surviving text devoted to epilepsy, usually dated 450–400 BCE; Alcmaeon and Democritus may have written earlier.

sources.citation: The evolution of the concepts of seizures and epilepsy: what's in a name? (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: Hippocratic collection, around 400 BC, by an unknown physician; scientific view of epilepsy.

sources.citation: From phenomena to phrasing: rethinking seizure classification through history (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: Epilepsy 'no more sacred than any other disease'; natural, brain-based causes; described signs; phlegm mechanism.

sources.citation: Alcmaeon. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Summer 2015 edition).
sources.supports: Alcmaeon's identification of the brain as the seat of intelligence influenced On the Sacred Disease.

title: Medical manuscripts buried at Mawangdui
summary: A Han-dynasty tomb at Mawangdui, sealed in 168 BCE, held the earliest surviving Chinese medical manuscripts, including a formulary of more than 250 prescriptions now called Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments.
explanation:
Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, near Changsha, probably belonged to Li Xi, a young nobleman of the Western Han. When it was excavated in 1973, a lacquer case in the coffin chamber held a library of texts written on silk, bamboo and wood. Among them were medical manuscripts that had been unknown for two thousand years.

The best known, now called Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments, contains more than 250 prescriptions and treatments. Other manuscripts deal with the body's channels and with treatment by moxa, a plant material burned on or near the skin. Because they predate the classic medical canons, they show Chinese medicine at an earlier, less systematised stage.

The tomb gives a firm latest date; the texts themselves were composed and copied earlier, at dates that are uncertain.

date.basis: The tomb was sealed in 168 BCE, so the manuscripts were written before then. When the texts were composed is uncertain.

locations.name: Mawangdui Tomb 3, near Changsha (Kingdom of Changsha)

whatChanged: Revealed medical writing from before the classic Chinese canons, otherwise lost.
whyItMattered: Changed scholars' understanding of how Chinese medicine developed and when its classic texts were compiled.
limitations: These are the earliest surviving manuscripts, not the beginning of Chinese medical writing.
How well the remedies worked is unknown, and they reflect ideas about illness very different from today's.

sources.citation: Raphals L. Review of Donald Harper, Early Chinese Medical Literature: The Mawangdui Medical Manuscripts (London: Kegan Paul, 1998). Project MUSE.
sources.supports: Seven medical manuscripts on three sheets of silk from Mawangdui Tomb 3, recovered in 1973; burial dated 168 BCE; first published 1983.

sources.citation: Introducing the *Wu ze you xing tu manuscript from Mawangdui. Early China (Cambridge University Press), 2020.
sources.supports: Tomb 3 at Changsha probably belonged to Li Xi (d. 168 BCE); manuscripts including medical texts on bamboo, wood and silk stored in a lacquer case.

sources.citation: Illness, remedies and medical care in Han China. Ancient History Sites.
sources.supports: Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments contains more than 250 prescriptions; other texts on bodily channels and moxa.

title: The Compendium of Suśruta describes surgery, including rebuilding the nose
summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā, a Sanskrit medical treatise composed in layers about two thousand years ago, is a foundation of Ayurveda and contains detailed surgical instructions, including the reconstruction of noses and ears with skin flaps.
explanation:
The Compendium of Suśruta is one of the classical texts of South Asian medicine. It covers diagnosis and therapy but is especially known for its surgical teaching, including the plastic repair of the nose and ears.

Its nasal reconstruction, using a flap of the patient's own skin, was later known in Europe as the 'Indian method'. The text was written in several authorial layers, and later commentators worked with revised versions. The oldest dated manuscript, from 878 CE and preserved in Kathmandu, records an earlier version than modern printed editions.

Popular and clinical literature often dates Suśruta to 600 BCE or even earlier. Philological research does not support these dates.

date.basis: The Suśruta Project dates the work to about two thousand years ago and stresses its many authorial layers; internal evidence suggests it is later than the Carakasaṃhitā. The earliest dated manuscript is from 878 CE. The range shown is deliberately broad.

locations.name: South Asia (place of composition unknown)
locations.role: Where the text was composed is not known

locationNote: No reliable place of composition is known, so the treatise appears in the list and timeline but not on the map. Its oldest dated manuscript is preserved in Kathmandu.

people.name: Suśruta (traditional author) and later redactors
people.role: Authors of successive layers of the text

whatChanged: Set down a systematic surgical curriculum and techniques such as flap repair of the nose.
whyItMattered: The Indian method of nasal reconstruction influenced European plastic surgery, and the text remains central to Ayurveda.
limitations: The common clinical claim that Suśruta lived around 600 BCE (or 1000–800 BCE) is not supported by textual scholarship.
The surviving text mixes layers from different periods, so not every technique can be dated to the same time.
contested: Dates for Suśruta and the Compendium vary by more than a millennium across publications; philologists date the work to about two thousand years ago.

sources.citation: The Suśruta Project (University of Alberta), project overview.
sources.supports: Written in Sanskrit about two thousand years ago; foundation of Ayurveda; MS Kathmandu KL 699 reliably datable to 878 CE; UNESCO Memory of the World.

sources.citation: Wujastyk D, Birch J, Klebanov A, et al. On the Plastic Surgery of the Ears and Nose: The Nepalese Version of the Suśrutasaṃhitā. Heidelberg Asian Studies Publishing, 2023.
sources.supports: Critical edition and translation of the chapter on plastic surgery of the ears and nose; differences between the Nepalese and later versions.

sources.supports: The Suśrutasaṃhitā has many authorial layers.

title: Tetracycline in the bones of ancient Nubians
summary: Bones from a population that lived in Sudanese Nubia around 350–550 CE contain the antibiotic tetracycline, probably from fermented grain or beer. Whether its use was deliberate is debated.
explanation:
In 1980, examining Nubian bones under ultraviolet light, the anthropologist George Armelagos and colleagues noticed a green-yellow fluorescence typical of tetracycline, an antibiotic produced by Streptomyces soil bacteria. Sceptics argued that the signal could have come from microbes invading the bones after burial.

In 2010, the chemist Mark Nelson and colleagues dissolved samples and confirmed by mass spectrometry that tetracycline was embedded in the bone itself, including in a young child. The quantities suggested regular consumption over long periods. The team proposed that the source was grain fermented into a beer-like gruel and contaminated with Streptomyces.

The authors believe the Nubians knew what they were doing. That is an interpretation: the chemistry shows exposure, not intention or medical purpose.

date.basis: Date range of the burial population studied (the 'X-Group' period).

locationNote: The burial sites lie in Sudanese Nubia; the marker shows the region rather than a specific cemetery.

people.name: Nubian communities of the Nile valley
people.role: Produced and consumed the fermented food or drink

people.name: George Armelagos
people.role: Bioarchaeologist who first noticed the fluorescence

whatChanged: Showed that people ingested an antibiotic substance some 1,500 years before antibiotics were discovered in the laboratory.
whyItMattered: Raises the possibility that fermented foods were used, knowingly or not, in ways that affected infection, and shows how chemistry can test archaeological claims.
limitations: The evidence shows consumption, not that the substance was used as medicine or that it improved health.
The claim that Nubians deliberately produced it is the researchers' interpretation.
contested: Earlier critics attributed the fluorescence to post-burial contamination; the 2010 chemical analysis addressed that, but the question of intent remains open.

sources.citation: Emory University. Ancient brewmasters tapped drug secrets. Emory Report, 31 August 2010.
sources.supports: Armelagos's 1980 discovery in Nubian bones dated 350–550 CE; regular consumption likely through beer; Nelson's analysis; researchers' view that use was deliberate.

sources.citation: Nelson ML, et al. Brief communication: mass spectroscopic characterization of tetracycline in the skeletal remains of an ancient population from Sudanese Nubia 350–550 CE. American Journal of Physical Anthropology 2010 (abstract as quoted by Phys.org and others).
sources.supports: Prior histological evidence (Bassett et al., 1980) met with scepticism over taphonomic contamination; acid extraction and mass spectroscopic confirmation; source tied to grain containing Streptomyces.

sourceNote: The findings come from one research group's work over several decades; no independent re-analysis was found.

title: Two thousand years of skull surgery in the Andes
summary: More trepanned skulls are known from Peru than from the rest of the world combined. Healing on the bone shows survival improved over time, reaching high rates in the centuries before the Spanish conquest.
explanation:
Over 800 skulls with surgical openings have been recovered from burial caves and excavations in coastal and highland Peru, the earliest dating to around 400 BCE. Analysing healing around the openings, John Verano and colleagues showed that early practitioners lost about half their patients, but that techniques were refined over the centuries.

Between about 1000 and 1400 CE, survival rose to as high as 91 per cent in some samples, and in the Inca period only around 17 to 25 per cent of patients died before their skulls began to heal. Some skulls bear several openings.

The researchers note that these outcomes compare favourably with nineteenth-century cranial surgery, but there are no written records explaining how Andean practitioners avoided infection.

date.basis: From the earliest dated trepanned crania studied (c. 400 BCE) to the end of the Inca period at the Spanish conquest.

locations.name: Central Andes: coastal and highland Peru

people.name: Andean practitioners across many cultures, including the Inca
John W. Verano, Anne Titelbaum and David Kushner

whatChanged: Documents a long, evolving surgical tradition in which outcomes measurably improved.
whyItMattered: Shows independent development of cranial surgery in the Americas, and that pre-modern surgeons could achieve high survival.
limitations: Healing shows survival, not why the operation was done or whether it helped the patient's condition.
Most skulls were collected in the late 1800s and early 1900s, and their contexts are not always well recorded.

sources.citation: Kushner DS, Verano JW, Titelbaum AR. Trepanation procedures/outcomes: comparison of prehistoric Peru with other ancient, medieval, and American Civil War cranial surgery. World Neurosurgery 2018;114.
sources.supports: More prehistoric trepanned crania in Peru than anywhere; nearly 2,000 years of practice from 400 BC; survival rates analysed.

sources.citation: University of Miami. Remarkable skill of ancient Peru's cranial surgeons. News release via ScienceDaily, 8 June 2018.
sources.supports: Over 800 skulls mostly collected in the late 1800s and early 1900s; survival up to 91% in some samples 1000–1400 CE; Verano's book Holes in the Head.

sources.citation: University of Miami News. Holes in the head (June 2018).
sources.supports: More trepanned skulls in Peru than the rest of the world combined; Inca survival about twice that of the American Civil War.

sources.citation: Live Science. The Incas mastered the grisly practice of drilling holes in people's skulls (2018).

title: Covered drains in every street of Mohenjo-daro
summary: In the third millennium BCE, the Indus city of Mohenjo-daro was built with drains along every street and lane, connected to bathing floors and wastewater chutes in houses.
explanation:
Mohenjo-daro, on the right bank of the Indus, is the best-preserved city of the Indus civilisation. Its lower town was laid out on a strict plan. Street drains of fitted baked brick, sealed with mud mortar, ran along every street and lane, even in the poorest quarters, and were mostly covered with bricks or limestone blocks that could be lifted for cleaning. Larger drains had corbelled roofs high enough for workers to enter.

Inside houses, bathing floors and vertical pipes in the walls carried wastewater out to the street drains. The same drains were maintained and rebuilt over long periods. The so-called Great Bath, a large waterproofed tank, was emptied through a covered drain.

The system shows organised management of water and waste on an urban scale. What its builders understood about the link between waste and disease is unknown.

date.basis: UNESCO dates the city to the 3rd millennium BCE. The drains were built and rebuilt over a long period within this range.

people.name: Inhabitants and builders of the Indus city

whatChanged: Shows city-wide management of wastewater built into urban design.
whyItMattered: One of the earliest known examples of sanitation planned at the scale of a whole city.
limitations: We cannot tell whether health was a motive; the drains may reflect ideas of cleanliness, ritual or simple practicality.
Similar features exist at other Indus cities such as Harappa; Mohenjo-daro is the best preserved, not necessarily the first.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro (List no. 138).
sources.supports: Most ancient and best preserved urban ruin in the Indus Valley, 3rd millennium BC; strictly planned lower town.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. State of conservation report, Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro.
sources.supports: Located on the right bank of the Indus, 28 km from Larkana; best preserved urban settlement in South Asia.

sources.citation: Harappa.com (J. M. Kenoyer and colleagues). Mohenjo-daro street with drains.
sources.supports: All streets and lanes had drains; vertical pipes and bathing-floor drains in houses; baked-brick drains sealed with mud mortar, mostly covered; reuse over time (Possehl).

sources.citation: Harappa.com. Ancient Indus city drains (quoting John Marshall).
sources.supports: Elaborate drainage even in the poorest quarters; removable brick or stone covers; corbelled roofs.

sources.citation: Harappa.com. Mohenjo-daro Great Bath diagram.
sources.supports: Great Bath's waste water carried off through a covered drain.

title: Ötzi the Iceman carried a medicinal fungus
summary: Ötzi, a man who died in the Alps around 3300 BCE, carried two pieces of birch polypore fungus strung on a leather thong. His gut contained whipworm eggs, and some researchers argue he used the fungus, which has antibacterial and anti-parasite properties, as medicine.
explanation:
Ötzi's body was found in 1991 in a glacier on the border between Austria and Italy, preserved with his clothing and equipment. Examination showed that he had been infected with whipworm, an intestinal parasite, as well as other ailments.

Among his belongings were two fragments of the birch polypore (Fomitopsis betulina), pierced and threaded on a strip of leather. In 1998 the palaeopathologist Luigi Capasso suggested in The Lancet that Ötzi used it as a natural laxative and antibiotic, perhaps against the worms. The fungus has a long history in European folk medicine, and laboratory studies have found antibacterial and anti-inflammatory compounds in it.

people.name: Ötzi
people.role: The man found in the ice

people.name: Luigi Capasso
people.role: Palaeopathologist who proposed the medicinal interpretation

whatChanged: It offers a possible glimpse of a prehistoric person carrying a natural remedy for his own ailments.
whyItMattered: Ötzi's equipment is among the oldest direct evidence that people may have carried medicines with them.
limitations: There is no direct evidence of how Ötzi used the fungus; other purposes are possible.
Fungi with medicinal properties may have been used much earlier, but such evidence rarely survives.
contested: Whether the fungus was medicine is debated: some researchers see a 'medicine kit', while others doubt that it was used for treatment at all.

sources.citation: Life and diseases of the Neolithic glacier mummy 'Ötzi'. Springer living reference work (2020).
sources.supports: Dated to c. 3350–3100 BCE; infected with whipworm (Trichuris trichiura); references to Capasso L, Lancet 352:1864 (1998), 'the Ice Man used natural laxatives and antibiotics'.

sources.citation: Pleszczyńska M, et al. Fomitopsis betulina (formerly Piptoporus betulinus): the Iceman's polypore fungus with modern biotechnological potential. World J Microbiol Biotechnol (2017).
sources.supports: Ötzi, who lived 5,300 years ago, carried two fragments of F. betulina; some scientists believe he used it medically (Capasso 1998), though the idea is controversial (Pöder 2005); long tradition of folk-medicine use.

sources.citation: Nature's first aid kit: a fungus growing on the side of birch trees. The Conversation (2019).

title: Specialist physicians at the Egyptian royal court
summary: Inscriptions from Egypt's Old Kingdom give physicians specialised titles. Iry, a Sixth Dynasty court doctor (c. 2300 BCE), was physician of the eyes and of the belly and 'shepherd of the king's rectum'. Two thousand years later Herodotus wrote that every Egyptian physician treated a single disease.
explanation:
Egyptian physicians (swnw) held ranked titles, and some were associated with particular parts of the body. Iry's inscriptions describe him as senior physician of the palace, physician of the eyes and of the belly, and guardian of the royal rectum, a role that included giving enemas to the king.

A study of known Egyptian physicians found that 12 of 42 from the Old Kingdom held titles indicating a speciality, and some claimed several. When Herodotus visited Egypt in the fifth century BCE he reported that medicine was divided so that each physician treated one disorder only, although historians treat this claim with caution.

date.basis: Iry served under the Sixth Dynasty (c. 2345–2181 BCE); Herodotus wrote in the fifth century BCE.

locationNote: Mapped to Giza, where a door inscribed with the titles of a physician of this kind was found.

people.name: Herodotus
people.role: Greek historian who described Egyptian medicine

whatChanged: Medical work was divided among practitioners with recognised areas of expertise.
whyItMattered: Egypt offers some of the earliest evidence of an organised medical profession with specialists.
limitations: Titles may describe court roles rather than specialist training in the modern sense.
Herodotus visited about two thousand years later, and his claim that each doctor treated only one disease is exaggerated: many physicians held several titles.

sources.citation: Fischer H. Pharaoh's proctologist: the Shepherd of the Rectum. Hektoen International (2023).
sources.supports: The physician (swnw) was typically a specialist; in the Sixth Dynasty (2345–2181 BC) Iry was awarded the title 'Shepherd of the King's Rectum'; enemas given to the pharaoh; Scholtz on Iry as an early eye doctor.

sources.citation: Early specialization in ancient Egyptian medicine and its possible relation to an archetypal image of the human organism. Medical History (Cambridge Core).
sources.supports: Old Kingdom: 42 known physicians, 12 with specialist titles, 3 with more than one; Herodotus's statement that each physician treats a single disorder should be treated with suspicion.

sources.citation: Ancient Egyptian pharaohs had a Shepherd of the Royal Anus. Ancient Origins.
sources.supports: Inscriptions describing a senior physician of the great house, physician of the belly, physician of the eyes and protector of the anus; Irynachet's titles found on a door at a Giza shaft tomb.

title: The Nineveh Medical Encyclopaedia in Ashurbanipal's library
summary: In the seventh century BCE scholars of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled at Nineveh a structured medical handbook of about fifty tablets, arranged in treatises from head to foot, with thousands of symptoms and prescriptions drawn from older Babylonian tradition.
explanation:
Mesopotamian medicine had been written down for more than a thousand years, and Ashurbanipal, who reigned from 669 to about 630 BCE, set out to collect all scholarly knowledge in his library. His scholars edited existing medical texts into new standard editions and arranged them, according to a surviving ancient catalogue, into a series of twelve treatises.

The tablets were broken when Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE and lay buried until excavated in the nineteenth century; many are now in the British Museum. Only recently have researchers reconstructed the whole encyclopaedia from its fragments.

date.basis: Compiled during the reign of Ashurbanipal.

whatChanged: Medical knowledge was gathered into a single systematic, organised reference work.
whyItMattered: It is described as the most standardised and systematic body of medical writing known before Galen.
limitations: It drew on earlier Babylonian texts; much of its content is older than the library.
Remedies were combined with incantations and ritual.

sources.citation: British Museum blog. Ancient healthcare fit for a king.
sources.supports: A 2,600-year-old handbook with thousands of descriptions of diseases and symptoms and prescriptions; compiled in the library of Ashurbanipal; made up of 12 sections.

sources.citation: Wellcome. Introducing Assyrian medicine: healthcare fit for a king (2019 award).
sources.supports: The world's most standardised, structured and systematised corpus of pre-Galenic medical literature; from the library of Ashurbanipal (669–c. 630 BCE); existence recognised only recently through a reconstructed ancient catalogue.

sources.citation: UCL. Introducing Assyrian Medicine: healthcare fit for a king.
sources.supports: Tablets broken into fragments during the sack of Nineveh in 612 BC; seventh-century BCE Royal Library of Ashurbanipal.

sources.citation: Simkó K. Weaving together loose threads: on the serialisation of the therapeutic corpus at Nineveh. KASKAL (2024).

title: Hammurabi's laws set surgeons' fees and penalties
summary: The law code of Hammurabi, king of Babylon around 1755 BCE, fixed what a physician could charge for a successful operation with a bronze lancet, according to the patient's status, and decreed that a surgeon whose operation killed a free man should lose his hand.
explanation:
Among the code's 282 laws, a group from §215 deals with healers. A physician who saved a free man's life by a major operation, or saved his eye by opening it with a bronze lancet, received ten shekels of silver; less was paid for a commoner or a slave. Setting a broken bone earned five shekels from a free man.

If the operation killed a free man or destroyed his eye, the physician's hand was to be cut off; if a slave died, he had to replace the slave.

date.basis: Hammurabi reigned c. 1792–1750 BCE; the code dates from late in his reign.

whatChanged: Medical treatment was regulated by law, with fixed fees and penalties for harm.
whyItMattered: It is among the earliest known legal rules on medical fees and liability for harm to patients.
limitations: The laws show how surgery was regulated, not how often operations were done or how they were performed.
Penalties and fees depended on social class, so patients were not treated equally.

sources.citation: NinMed (ORACC, University of Pennsylvania). Surgery: information from texts, quoting Roth 1995.
sources.supports: §215: a physician who heals a person after a serious wound with a bronze lancet, or saves an eye, takes 10 shekels; §218: if he causes death or blinds the eye, they shall cut off his hand; patients paid healers.

sources.citation: Document 1.1: Hammurabi's laws for physicians. Bedford/St Martin's (Hunt, The Making of the West).
sources.supports: In Hammurabi's 282 laws, fees for successful operations and punishment for errors; law 218, cutting off the hand.

sources.citation: Managed Care magazine. Here are sections of the code and the fees prescribed.

title: The Ebers Papyrus and Egypt's other medical papyri
summary: The Ebers Papyrus, a 20-metre scroll written in Egypt around 1550 BCE, is the most extensive surviving record of ancient Egyptian medicine. It gathers some 700 remedies and spells and a treatise on the heart and its vessels. Other papyri, such as the Hearst, London and Berlin papyri, preserve related texts.
explanation:
The scroll's 110 pages hold some 700 magical formulas and folk remedies, for complaints ranging from crocodile bites to toenail pain, as well as a treatise on the heart and its vessels and a chapter on disorders such as depression. A calendar on the back mentions the ninth year of King Amenhotep I. It was reportedly found in a tomb in the Assasif area of the Theban necropolis and was bought by the Egyptologist Georg Ebers, who published it in 1875.

Later medical papyri overlap with it: the Hearst Papyrus from the reign of Thutmose III; the London Medical Papyrus, dated to Tutankhamun's reign; and the Berlin or Brugsch Papyrus of about 1300 BCE.

date.basis: Dated by a calendar referring to year 9 of Amenhotep I; the other papyri date from c. 1450 to 1300 BCE.

people.name: Georg Ebers
people.role: Egyptologist who bought and published the papyrus

people.name: Edwin Smith
people.role: American dealer in Luxor who owned it first

whatChanged: It preserves the fullest picture of how Egyptian doctors understood and treated disease.
whyItMattered: The Egyptian medical papyri are among the oldest medical books to survive, giving a detailed picture of a medical tradition that combined practical remedies with magic.
limitations: It is believed to be copied from earlier texts, so its contents are older than the scroll.
Its circumstances of discovery rest on a dealer's account and are uncertain.

sources.citation: Strukturen und Transformationen des Wortschatzes der ägyptischen Sprache (Saxon Academy of Sciences, Leipzig). Papyrus Edwin Smith: metadata and provenance.
sources.supports: The Ebers papyrus's find spot unknown, but the seller told Ebers it came from a tomb in the Assasif, in a coffin between the legs of a mummy; Edwin Smith in Luxor.

title: Saffron frescoes at Akrotiri on Thera
summary: Wall paintings in the building called Xeste 3 at Akrotiri, a Bronze Age town on Thera (Santorini) buried by a volcanic eruption around 1600 BCE, show women gathering saffron crocus flowers and offering them to a goddess. Some scholars interpret them as the earliest images of a medicinal plant being prepared.
explanation:
The frescoes show girls and women picking crocuses in a rocky landscape and bringing them in baskets to a seated goddess, flanked by a griffin and a monkey. Xeste 3 was a large, richly decorated building, probably used for rituals.

In 2004 the art historian Susan Ferrence and the cardiologist Gordon Bendersky argued that the scenes depict the stages of producing saffron as a drug and show a goddess of healing. Saffron was later used in medicine, appearing in the Ebers Papyrus and in Dioscorides' first-century herbal.

date.basis: The town flourished around 1600 BCE before it was buried by the eruption of Thera.

people.name: Susan Ferrence and Gordon Bendersky
people.role: Researchers who proposed the medicinal interpretation

whatChanged: If the interpretation is right, the frescoes show a plant being gathered and processed for its healing value.
whyItMattered: They are cited as possible early visual evidence for the medicinal use of plants in the Mediterranean.
limitations: Earlier studies of the frescoes relied mainly on the images themselves, which can support several readings.
Saffron was also valued as a dye, food and ritual offering.
contested: Whether the frescoes show medicine is disputed: they have also been read as scenes of ritual and fertility, or of perfume and spice production.

sources.citation: Day J. Crocuses in context: a diachronic survey of the crocus motif in the Aegean Bronze Age. Hesperia 80(3):337 (2011).
sources.supports: Discoveries at Akrotiri in the 1960s added frescoes featuring the crocus; potential medicinal powers and ritual roles debated; Xeste 3 frescoes the sole basis for Ferrence and Bendersky (2004) and others.

sources.citation: Stone Pages archaeology news. Ancient frescoes show early medicinal use of saffron.
sources.supports: Frescoes once thought to show perfume or spice production; Ferrence and Bendersky's view that they show stages of saffron production and a goddess of healing.

sources.citation: Saffron: an oxytocic? O&G Magazine (RANZCOG).
sources.supports: Xeste 3 frescoes depict women in ritual scenes with Crocus sativus; a goddess flanked by a griffin and a blue monkey; medicinal use of saffron noted in the Ebers Papyrus and by Dioscorides.

sources.citation: Museum of Cycladic Art. The fresco of women from the 'adyton' of Xeste 3, Akrotiri, Thera.
sources.supports: Xeste 3 at Akrotiri flourished in 1600 BC; saffron-gatherers collecting crocuses to offer to Potnia, goddess of nature and fertility.

title: Udjahorresnet restores the medical 'House of Life' at Sais
summary: Around 519 BCE the Persian king Darius I sent the Egyptian chief physician Udjahorresnet back to Egypt to restore the 'House of Life' at Sais, a temple institution where physicians were trained and texts kept. His inscribed statue, now in the Vatican, records the commission.
explanation:
Udjahorresnet, whose titles included chief physician, treasurer and commander of the king's fleet, served the Persian kings who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE. According to the inscription on his naophorous statue (a figure holding a small shrine), Darius ordered him to return home and restore the houses of life that had fallen into ruin.

One recent study links the order to Darius's dissatisfaction with Egyptian physicians, who, according to Herodotus, had failed to cure his injured ankle.

date.basis: Darius I came to the throne in 522 BCE; the statue was probably made soon after Udjahorresnet's return.

people.name: Udjahorresnet
people.role: Chief physician and priest of Neith

whatChanged: A royal order restored an institution for training physicians and keeping medical texts.
whyItMattered: It is one of the clearest records of an ancient state supporting medical education.
limitations: The nature of the House of Life is debated; it was a temple scriptorium and school, not a medical school in the modern sense.
The statue's provenance is assumed rather than known.

sources.citation: Livius.org. Wedjahor-Resne (Udjahorresnet) and his inscription.
sources.supports: Naophoros statue about 70 cm high, brought to Italy by Hadrian, now in the Vatican Museums; Darius allowed him to return and ordered him to supervise the destroyed 'houses of life'; statue probably made soon after his return.

sources.citation: Vatican Museums. The 'Vatican Naophorous'.
sources.supports: Statue of Udjahorresnet, chief physician and commander of the king's fleet, holding a naos; provenance unknown but assumed to be Sais.

sources.citation: Udjahorresnet, Democedes and Darius I: the reform of the House of Life as consequence of the Egyptian physicians' failure to heal the Achaemenid ruler. Journal of the Egyptian Expedition.
sources.supports: Comparison of Herodotus III.129–130 with the statue; Darius's dislocated ankle healed by Democedes; the king ordered Udjahorresnet to restore the House of Life at Sais and/or throughout Egypt; 522–519 BCE.

title: Medicinal tablets survive in a Roman-era shipwreck
summary: A ship that sank off Populonia in Tuscany around 140 BCE carried a physician's supplies, including a tin box of flat grey tablets. Chemical analysis published in 2013 showed they were mainly zinc compounds mixed with starch, fats and pine resin, probably an eye medicine.
explanation:
The Pozzino wreck, found in 1974 in the Gulf of Baratti and excavated in 1989–90, held a small mortar, a bronze cupping vessel, an iron probe, 136 wooden vials and many tin boxes, evidently a medical kit.

Researchers analysed the discoid tablets, each about 4 cm across, and found that the zinc minerals hydrozincite and smithsonite made up most of their mineral content. Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides describe zinc compounds being used for the eyes and skin, and the tablets' shape matches the Latin collyrium, from a Greek word for small round loaves, used for eye remedies.

date.basis: The wreck is dated to the second century BCE, about 140 BCE.

whatChanged: It provides physical evidence of a manufactured medicine in measured, portable doses.
whyItMattered: Ancient medicines rarely survive; these tablets let researchers compare ancient recipes with an actual preparation.
limitations: Written recipes for pills and tablets are known from earlier sources; this is a rare surviving example, not the first use.
How the tablets were used is inferred from their composition and from ancient texts.

sources.citation: Giachi G, Pallecchi P, Romualdi A, et al. Ingredients of a 2,000-y-old medicine revealed by chemical, mineralogical, and botanical investigations. PNAS 110(4):1193–1196 (2013).
sources.supports: Tin pyxis from the Pozzino shipwreck (second century BC) with six flat grey discoid tablets; hydrozincite and smithsonite the most abundant ingredients, with starch, lipids and pine resin; probably ophthalmic, the collyrium.

sources.citation: Mariotti Lippi M, Giachi G. Pollen content in a II century BC remedy from the Pozzino shipwreck. Palynology 45(1) (2021).
sources.supports: Wreck in the Gulf of Baratti near Piombino at about 18 m, near Etruscan Populonia; mortar, bronze cupping vessel, iron probe, tin pyxides and 136 wooden vials.

sources.citation: Digging up ancient drug formulations. Chemistry World (2013).
sources.supports: Discovered in 1974 and excavated in 1989–1990; zinc around 75% of the sample; Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides describe zinc compounds for eyes and skin.

sources.supports: The hull dated to about 140 BC; tablets may have been eye medicine.
